cards.front: What are the two forms of type information in Java?
cards.back: Compile-time RTTI (casts, instanceof) and reflection (types discovered at run time)
cards.extra: Traditional RTTI assumes every type is known when you compile. Reflection lets a program open a class it has never seen and inspect or invoke it.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
    Object o = "hi";
    System.out.println(o instanceof String + " " + (String) o + " " + o.getClass().getMethod("length").getName()); // compile-time RTTI and runtime reflection
  }
}

cards.back: The Class object representing its actual runtime type
cards.extra: It ignores the reference type — a Shape reference to a Circle returns Circle.class. That object is the entry point to all reflection.
cards.example:
Object o = "hi";
Class c = o.getClass();
System.out.println(c.getName()); // java.lang.String: the actual runtime type

cards.extra: The compiler only knows the reference type, so it cannot prove the object's real class. That runtime check is the most basic form of RTTI.
cards.example:
Object o = "hi";
String s = (String) o; // runtime check succeeds
try { Integer n = (Integer) o; } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("wrong cast"); }

cards.front: What does instanceof test, and how does it differ from comparing Class objects?
cards.back: instanceof includes subclasses; Class equality is the exact type only
cards.extra: circle instanceof Shape is true because Circle IS-A Shape. circle.getClass() == Shape.class is false — a different question.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static class Base {}
  static class Sub extends Base {}
  public static void main(String[] a) { Object o = new Sub(); System.out.println((o instanceof Base) + " " + (o.getClass() == Base.class)); }
}

cards.back: Loads and initialises that class from a string at run time
cards.extra: The compiler never saw the name, which is the point: configuration files, plugin names and JDBC drivers are loaded this way.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static { System.out.println("initialised"); }
  public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception { Class.forName("Ex"); }
}

cards.front: What is reflection actually used for?
cards.back: Discovering methods and fields, and invoking them, without compile-time knowledge of the class
cards.extra: Frameworks rely on it: Spring wires beans by name, JUnit finds @Test methods, serialisers read fields. The cost is safety and speed.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  public int n = 7;
  public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
    Object o = new Ex(); System.out.println(o.getClass().getField("n").get(o) + " " + o.getClass().getMethod("toString").invoke(o));
  }
}

cards.front: Why does reflection feel dangerous compared to normal code?
cards.back: Every mistake moves from compile time to runtime — no type checking, no refactoring support
cards.extra: A misspelled method name compiles fine and fails when invoked. That is the trade for extensibility without recompilation.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  public static void main(String[] a) {
    Object o = "hi";
    try { o.getClass().getMethod("lenght"); } catch (NoSuchMethodException e) { System.out.println("compiles, fails at runtime"); }
  }
}
